prompt: Large quantities of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans every year. What do you think are the main reasons for this, and what could be done to address the situation?
essay:
The image of plastic in the ocean invites a tidy explanation — careless people, missing bins — and a correspondingly tidy remedy in more recycling. Both are misleading. Recycling has been promoted for four decades while the volume entering the sea has continued to rise, which suggests the mechanism producing the waste is not one that collection can outpace.

That mechanism is a price gap. Making new plastic from oil is cheaper than recovering, sorting and reprocessing the plastic already in circulation, and it is cheaper by a margin that no amount of civic enthusiasm closes. A material worth almost nothing once used will be dropped, buried or informally burned wherever collecting it costs more than it returns, and rivers do the rest. Compounding this, the countries now receiving the largest volumes of packaging are frequently those whose waste systems were built for a different, mostly organic, waste stream and were never funded to expand at the speed consumption did.

If the gap is the cause, closing it is the solution. Extended producer responsibility — obliging the company that puts packaging on the market to pay for its recovery — converts an externality into a line on a balance sheet, and firms respond to costs on balance sheets in a way they do not respond to appeals. Deposit schemes work by the same logic from the other end, giving a discarded bottle enough residual value that somebody will trouble to return it.

The objection is that these costs are ultimately passed to consumers, and they are. But they are being paid already, in fisheries, tourism and clean-up budgets, by people who had no part in the transaction. Moving that cost back to the point of sale does not create it. It simply puts it where a decision can be made about it.
title: Plastic waste reaching the oceans
